prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength and bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from the two-part B022 plus B003 to B022 alone. The lattice clock is a single, sharply defined invention with the cleanest allocation on the shortlist: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and first realised it, and Ye brought many-body control and the 10^-18 regime. It has been reproduced and surpassed in independent laboratories, compared over fibre links, and it feeds into tests of relativity and of the constancy of constants, dark-matter searches and relativistic geodesy. On the lineage objection, I think the citation can state the difference: the 2005 prize rewarded the frequency comb as a tool and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock interrogates many neutral atoms at once and has its own physics. The discovery is at the centre, and here the people behind it can be named without leaving a visible hole in the credit.
statement.case_against: B022 is close to two earlier prizes in the optical-frequency-metrology lineage, and ion-clock groups and other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Gill, Lisdat and others) lie outside a two-name credit. The pending redefinition of the second is a timing caution, though I do not treat it as a flaw in the science. Dropping B003 also means setting aside the only candidate that opens a new observational window, and I still regard the IceCube flux as a real and secure discovery. I drop it for attribution, not for lack of science: the chair asked whether any defensible multi-name credit exists within the supplied names, and I must answer that none does, so a one-name award for a collaboration-scale discovery, with AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal outside it, is too thin to carry a prize part. Finally, B039 has the broadest committee support and a prize without it must explain why.

responses.point: The chair asked whether either of us still wants B003 in a preferred configuration, and has himself moved it to an alternative after the opening ballots.
responses.response: I follow you and withdraw B003 from my preferred configuration. In round 1 I said I would rather B022 or B039 stand alone if the attribution were judged too thin, and the exchange confirms that it is: no second name is available, and neither of us has found a defensible multi-name credit within the supplied names. I keep B003 as an alternative because the diffuse flux is secure and I do not want its deferral to be read as doubt about the discovery. I disagree gently with your reading that the second-detector point is minor, though; for a first-ever window it matters to me that one more independent confirmation arrives.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that B039 extends the 2016 prize to time-reversal-invariant systems because the new ingredient is spin-orbit-driven band inversion in a real material, and that it is the broadest-supported candidate.
responses.response: That is the best statement of what is new relative to 2016, and it answers the chair's question better than the general wording about topology. It moves me from ranking B039 fourth towards treating it as my first alternative. It does not move me to put it first, because the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is not a footnote: the HgTe proposal is what told Molenkamp what to measure, and a citation to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect leaves that visibly outside. I also do not think support counts decide this; five condensed-matter-leaning members agreeing is evidence about the field's view, but the credit problem is the same whoever counts it.

responses.point: Kroll defends B022 as a clean two-name allocation, concedes that topological insulators have wider influence, and asks that Ye's role be described as precision and many-body control, not only demonstration.
responses.response: I accept your request on Ye and have written the citation around realization at the 10^-18 level rather than a demonstration of the idea. I also take your concession on breadth seriously, and I agree that it is the honest comparison with B039: wider influence for topological insulators, a cleaner and more complete credit for the clock. Your point that the pending redefinition is irrelevant to merit is one I share in substance, but I would not dismiss it entirely, since formal redefinition would remove the one open maturity question and might change how some colleagues rank B022 against B039.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B039 because it is a new principle and fits the statute better than a technology whose value is mainly engineering performance, and he treats the lattice clock as precision metrology.
responses.response: I disagree that the lattice clock is only engineering performance. The magic-wavelength idea is a conceptual step: it removes the light shift as an obstacle to trapping, and the many-body control that Ye demonstrated is physics in its own right, which is why clocks now probe fundamental constants and gravitational redshift at the millimetre scale. I do agree with you that the committee should state plainly whether the B039 citation is for the 2D case, and I note that you and the other supporters now seem to accept that scoping. If that wording is adopted, my objection to B039 reduces to the missing credit, not to the science.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B022 first, stresses that ion-clock pioneers, Lemonde and other strontium groups have claims the supplied credit cannot settle, and says the clock is distinct from the comb and ion-control prizes.
responses.response: We agree on the central points, and your attribution caveat is the right limit on what B022 can claim. I would handle it in the citation, by naming the lattice concept and the accuracy frontier and not clocks in general, so that single-ion groups and other lattice groups are not implied to be excluded from the field's credit. Where I would press you is on the 2005 and 2012 lineage: you call the clock distinct, and I agree, but Eriksson and Mehlig describe it as a refinement, so the committee should be able to say in one sentence what the neutral-atom lattice adds, and I propose that it is many-atom interrogation at the magic wavelength.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a third recognition in the optical-frequency-metrology lineage after 2005 and 2012, and whether the one-sentence distinction I offer, many-atom interrogation at a magic wavelength, is defensible.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should change the ranking of B022 against B039 if it happens, and whether waiting for it would be wise.

Whether B039 can be given a 2D quantum spin Hall citation that does not look like a dismissal of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang; I rely on my own recollection of the priority history and have not verified it.
Whether B003 could return in a later year with a broader credit and a second detector confirming the diffuse flux.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: my documented connections are David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, none of whom is a credited name on any shortlisted ballot. I note that my own field is theory and cosmology, so I rely on colleagues in atomic physics and condensed matter for the detailed experimental record of B022 and B039. Kroll has disclosed a stay in Hall's laboratory; I see no recusal ground arising from it for B022.
